title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
authors: Greshake, Abdelnabi, Mishra, Endres, Holz, Fritz
central_claim: Defines indirect prompt injection: instructions planted in data the application retrieves later control the model remotely.
cite_claim: Data an LLM application retrieves can carry instructions; LLM-integrated apps blur data and instructions.
quote: We argue that LLM-Integrated Applications blur the line between data and instructions.
relevance: Foundational. fiks feeds vendor response bodies (attacker-controllable data) into the repair agent's prompt.

title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
authors: Debenedetti, Zhang, Balunovic, Beurer-Kellner, Fischer, Tramer
central_claim: 97 tasks and 629 security cases. Injections sit inside tool outputs. With GPT-4o, data delimiters cut targeted ASR only to 41.65%, while a tool filter cut it to 6.84%.
cite_claim: Prompt injections placed in tool results hijack agents. Delimiting defenses only partly reduce targeted ASR.
location: Sec. 3.1/App. A (attacks); Sec. 4.1, Table 3; Sec. 4.3, Table 5
quote: injections placed towards the end of a tool's response message are most effective
relevance: Primary harness for injecting payloads into tool outputs. The repair agent reads a tool output (the trace) as part of its prompt. The key is already in the bibliography.

title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents
central_claim: 1,054 test cases (17 user tools, 62 attacker tools); ReAct GPT-4 is vulnerable 24% of the time; a reinforcing 'hacking prompt' nearly doubles ASR.
cite_claim: Tool-integrated agents follow attacker instructions embedded in tool responses at non-trivial rates.
quote: ReAct-prompted GPT-4 vulnerable to attacks 24% of the time
relevance: Attack-string source for adversarial vendor bodies.

title: Agent Security Bench (ASB): Formalizing and Benchmarking Attacks and Defenses in LLM-based Agents
authors: Zhang, Huang, Mei, Yao, Wang, Zhan, Wang, Zhang
central_claim: Tests 10 scenarios, 400+ tools, and 27 attack and defense methods on 13 LLMs. The highest average ASR is 84.30%, and current defenses show limited effectiveness.
cite_claim: Across agent scenarios, prompt-injection, memory-poisoning and backdoor attacks reach high average ASR, and existing defenses are of limited effectiveness.
quote: with the highest average attack success rate of 84.30%, but limited effectiveness shown in current defenses
relevance: Breadth evidence that defenses that only filter inputs are weak. Motivates structural controls in fiks.

title: RedCode: Risky Code Execution and Generation Benchmark for Code Agents
authors: Guo, Liu, Xie, Zhou, Zeng, Lin, Song, Li
central_claim: RedCode-Exec has 4,050 risky Python/Bash cases across 25 vulnerability types, and RedCode-Gen has 160 prompts. Covers 3 agent frameworks and 19 LLMs. Agents reject risky operations given as natural text less often than those given as code.
cite_claim: Code agents often execute or generate risky code. Refusal depends on how the request is phrased.
quote: agents are more likely to reject executing risky operations on the operating system
relevance: Shows that the repair agent's own refusals are not a reliable control, so fiks needs out-of-model controls.

title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design (CaMeL)
authors: Debenedetti, Shumailov, Fan, Hayes, Carlini, Fabian, Kern, Shi, Terzis, Tramer
central_claim: Separates control flow, which comes from the trusted query, from untrusted data and adds capabilities. On AgentDojo it solves 77% of tasks with provable security, vs 84% undefended.
cite_claim: Separating data and control flow gives provable injection resistance at a modest utility cost.
quote: the untrusted data retrieved by the LLM can never impact the program flow.
relevance: The strongest version of data/control separation. fiks's repair loop has a fixed control flow but an LLM-chosen edit, so CaMeL applies only partly. The key is already in the bibliography.

title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
authors: Beurer-Kellner, Buesser, Cretu, Debenedetti, Dobos, Fabian, Fischer, Froelicher, Grosse, Naeff, Ozoani, Paverd, Tramer, Volhejn
central_claim: Proposes six patterns: Action-Selector, Plan-Then-Execute, LLM Map-Reduce, Dual LLM, Code-Then-Execute and Context-Minimization. A case study of a software-engineering agent recommends a Dual LLM with strictly formatted interfaces to untrusted docs or code.
cite_claim: Once untrusted input enters an agent, that input must be unable to trigger consequential actions. For coding agents, the safest design gives the agent only a strictly formatted view of untrusted content.
quote: the code agent only interacts with untrusted documentation or code by means of a strictly formatted interface
relevance: Gives fiks a concrete defence to implement: pass the repair agent a strictly typed trace diff instead of the raw vendor body. Basis for H-S2.

title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections
authors: Nasr, Carlini, Sitawarin, Schulhoff, Hayes, Ilie, Pluto, Song, Chaudhari, Shumailov, Thakurta, Xiao, Terzis, Tramer
central_claim: 12 recent defenses that reported near-zero ASR are bypassed with adaptive attacks at >90% ASR for most.
cite_claim: Prompt-injection defenses evaluated on static attacks fail under adaptive attacks. Security claims need adaptive evaluation.
quote: We bypass 12 recent defenses (based on a diverse set of techniques) with attack success rate above 90% for most
relevance: The strongest critique. Any fiks result on prompt-level defences such as spotlighting must be reported as a static-attack result only.

title: Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks With Spotlighting
authors: Hines, Lopez, Hall, Zarfati, Zunger, Kiciman
central_claim: Input transformations that signal provenance (delimiting, datamarking, encoding) reduce ASR from >50% to <2% on GPT-family models with minimal task impact.
cite_claim: Provenance marking of untrusted input can sharply cut injection ASR in static evaluations.
quote: The key insight is to utilize transformations of an input to provide a reliable and continuous signal of its provenance.
relevance: A cheap baseline defence for fiks prompts. Its results conflict with AgentDojo Table 5 and Nasr et al.

title: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection (OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications)
central_claim: Defines indirect prompt injection and lists mitigations: least privilege, human approval for high-risk actions, segregation of external content, and adversarial testing.
cite_claim: An industry standard taxonomy that recommends human approval for privileged actions and segregation of untrusted content.
location: Sections 'Types of Prompt Injection' and 'Prevention and Mitigation Strategies'
quote: Indirect prompt injections occur when an LLM accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files.
relevance: Maps directly onto fiks's controls: never merge (human approval), path allow-list (least privilege) and the trace prompt (segregation).

title: The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication
central_claim: An agent that combines private data access, exposure to untrusted content and an external communication channel can be made to exfiltrate data. MCP makes it easy to assemble that combination.
cite_claim: Agents combining private data, untrusted content and outbound channels are exfiltration-prone.
quote: an attacker can easily trick it into accessing your private data
relevance: fiks's repair step combines untrusted content (the vendor body), private data (the repo and env) and an outbound channel (git push, the PR body, CI, network from pnpm test). Framing for the threat model.

title: GitHub MCP Exploited: Accessing private repositories via MCP
central_claim: A malicious public GitHub issue hijacks an agent using the official GitHub MCP server. The agent leaks private-repo data into a PR on a public repo ('toxic agent flow'). It is an architectural issue, not a server bug.
cite_claim: Untrusted issue text read through MCP can make an agent write private data into a pull request.
location: Post body (26 May 2025), attack setup and mitigations sections
quote: hijack a user's agent via a malicious GitHub Issue
relevance: The closest real-world analog to fiks. Untrusted text enters a coding-capable agent whose output is a PR. Mitigation is scoping to one repository, which fiks does with one worktree. Quote was captured via the fetch summary [verify exact wording].

title: MCP Security Notification: Tool Poisoning Attacks
central_claim: Hidden instructions in MCP tool descriptions (tool poisoning), descriptions that change after approval (rug pull) and cross-server shadowing. Recommends pinning and hash-verifying tool descriptions.
cite_claim: MCP tool metadata is an injection channel. Pinning and checksums of tool descriptions mitigate rug pulls.
quote: Clients should pin the version of the MCP server and its tools to prevent unauthorized changes.
relevance: fiks sits between agent and server. The tool descriptions it proxies and the contracts it derives can be poisoned, so fiks should pin and hash them.

title: MCPTox: A Benchmark for Tool Poisoning Attack on Real-World MCP Servers
central_claim: 1,348 malicious cases over 45 live MCP servers and 353 tools on 20 agents. o1-mini ASR is 72.8%, and the highest refusal rate (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) is below 3%.
cite_claim: Tool poisoning on real MCP servers succeeds often and models rarely refuse.
quote: agents rarely refuse these attacks, with the highest refused rate (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) less than 3%
relevance: Real-server evidence that MCP-layer injection is effective. Supports treating everything from the server and vendor side as hostile in fiks.

title: GitHub Copilot: Remote Code Execution via Prompt Injection (CVE-2025-53773)
venue_or_publisher: Embrace The Red blog; MITRE CVE-2025-53773
central_claim: Injected content makes Copilot write chat.tools.autoApprove into .vscode/settings.json, which enables 'YOLO mode' and code execution. Patched in the August 2025 Patch Tuesday.
cite_claim: A coding agent that can edit its own configuration files can be prompt-injected into disabling its approval gate and executing code.
location: Post body (12 Aug 2025); CVE record published 2025-08-12
quote: placing Copilot into YOLO mode by modifying the project's settings.json file
relevance: Why fiks forbids edits outside src/ and passes settingSources: []. The agent must not reach its own permission config.

title: CVE-2025-54135: Cursor agent writes new dotfiles (.cursor/mcp.json) without approval, enabling RCE via indirect prompt injection
central_claim: Before Cursor 1.3.9, creating a new dotfile needed no approval. An indirect prompt injection could create .cursor/mcp.json and trigger RCE.
cite_claim: Indirect prompt injection let a coding agent create its own MCP config and gain code execution (CVE-2025-54135).
quote: an attacker can chain a indirect prompt injection vulnerability to hijack the context to write to the settings file and trigger RCE
relevance: Shows that 'creating' and 'editing' files must be governed by the same allow-list. fiks's mayWrite applies one regex to both.

title: CVE-2025-54794: Claude Code path restriction bypass via prefix matching
central_claim: Claude Code below 0.2.111 used prefix matching for its directory restriction. With untrusted content in context, files outside the CWD could be accessed.
cite_claim: A prefix-matching path check in a coding agent was bypassable when untrusted content reached its context (CVE-2025-54794).
quote: a path validation flaw using prefix matching instead of canonical path comparison, makes it possible to bypass directory restrictions
relevance: Directly relevant to fiks's own path allow-list. insideWorktree uses resolve and relative, not prefix matching, but symlinks are not canonicalised. This is a test case for the guard.

title: "Your AI, My Shell": Demystifying Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic AI Coding Editors
authors: Liu, Zhao, Lyu, Zhang, Wang, Lo
central_claim: AIShellJack has 314 payloads covering 70 MITRE ATT&CK techniques, delivered through poisoned rule files. ASR is up to 84% (Cursor auto mode). With terminal access restricted, 88.2% of cases still embedded malicious code in source files.
cite_claim: Restricting a coding agent's terminal is insufficient. Injected agents still write malicious code into source files.
quote: Thus, restricting terminal access alone is insufficient.
relevance: The strongest counter-argument to fiks's guard. fiks allows writes to src/ and then runs src via pnpm test and CI, so an injected payload can execute.

title: New Vulnerability in GitHub Copilot and Cursor: How Hackers Can Weaponize Code Agents (Rules File Backdoor)
central_claim: Invisible Unicode in rule files steers Copilot and Cursor to insert malicious code that reviewers miss. Both vendors first called it user responsibility. GitHub added a hidden-Unicode warning on 1 May 2025.
cite_claim: Hidden-Unicode instructions in repo config steer coding agents to inject code that human PR review misses.
quote: turning a developer's most trusted assistant into an unwitting accomplice
relevance: Human merge review, fiks's last line of defence, can miss invisible payloads. fiks should strip or flag non-printing characters in traces and diffs.

title: PromptPwnd: Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in GitHub Actions Using AI Agents
central_claim: CI workflows put untrusted issue, PR and commit text into prompts for AI agents (Gemini CLI, Claude Code Action, Codex) that hold privileged tokens. At least 5 Fortune-500 companies are affected, and Gemini CLI was patched within 4 days.
cite_claim: Feeding untrusted repository text to CI-hosted coding agents with privileged tokens lets attackers leak secrets or modify repos.
location: Post body (4 Dec 2025; updated 17 Mar 2026), mitigations list
quote: Live proof-of-concept exploits already exist, and several major open-source projects are affected.
relevance: The closest pattern to fiks running unattended. Untrusted text reaches a coding agent holding a GitHub token.

title: s1ngularity: supply chain attack leaks secrets on GitHub: everything you need to know
central_claim: Malicious Nx npm releases came from a pull_request_target workflow with injectable PR titles. The malware drove installed AI CLIs (Claude, Gemini, Q) with permission-skipping flags to hunt for secrets. More than 1,000 GitHub tokens leaked, and more than 5,500 repos were later made public.
cite_claim: Attackers already weaponize locally installed AI coding CLIs run with permission prompts disabled, and a CI title-injection bug seeded the compromise.
quote: the malware leveraged AI command-line tools (including Claude, Gemini, and Q) to aid in their reconnaissance efforts
relevance: Shows two fiks-relevant facts. Running an agent CLI with permission prompts disabled (fiks's fallback uses --permission-mode dontAsk with an allow-list) is a real attack target, and CI that consumes PR metadata is an entry point.

title: AWS-2025-015: Amazon Q Developer for VS Code extension security bulletin
central_claim: An over-scoped GitHub token in a CodeBuild configuration let a threat actor commit malicious code to the Amazon Q extension's repository. The code was auto-included in release 1.84.0, and 1.85.0 is the fix.
cite_claim: An over-privileged CI token let an attacker commit code to an AI coding-assistant repo that shipped automatically in a release.
quote: the threat actor was able to commit malicious code into the extension's open-source repository
relevance: Shows why fiks's GitHub credential must be least-privilege (branch push only, no release or workflow scope) and why auto-release after merge is risky.

title: Surprise: When Dependabot Contributes Malicious Code
central_claim: Using stolen PATs, attackers pushed commits styled as dependabot[bot] to hundreds of repos. The commits added a workflow that exfiltrated secrets and a form-credential stealer.
cite_claim: Attackers impersonate trusted dependency bots so that malicious commits get less scrutiny.
quote: Those commit messages were fabricated by threat actors to appear as a Dependabot automated contribution
relevance: Bot impersonation risk for a 'Dependabot for APIs'. A fiks PR must be verifiable (signed commits, GitHub App identity) or attackers can pose as fiks.

title: CVE-2024-3094: malicious code in xz/liblzma upstream tarballs
central_claim: The xz 5.6.0+ build extracts a prebuilt object from a disguised test file and uses it to modify liblzma functions.
cite_claim: Test files are a proven carrier for supply-chain payloads (xz, CVE-2024-3094).
quote: the liblzma build process extracts a prebuilt object file from a disguised test file existing in the source code
relevance: Closest real precedent for fixture poisoning. fiks commits attacker-supplied bytes (recorded vendor bodies, *.rerecorded.json) into the target repo's test/ tree.

title: Keeping your GitHub Actions and workflows secure Part 1: Preventing pwn requests
central_claim: pull_request_target workflows that check out and build untrusted PR code run it with a write token and secrets. Build scripts, tests and install hooks are code-execution vectors.
cite_claim: Any automated processing of untrusted PR code with privileged CI is dangerous. Tests and install hooks execute attacker code.
quote: Any automated processing of PRs from an external fork is potentially dangerous.
relevance: fiks's CI gate pushes agent-written code to a branch on the target repo, where push-triggered CI runs it with that repo's CI context before any human review.

title: OpenSSF Scorecard checks documentation (Code-Review, Branch-Protection, Dangerous-Workflow)
central_claim: Code-Review requires human review before merge, and bot reviews do not count. Branch-Protection requires reviews and status checks. Dangerous-Workflow flags pull_request_target combined with a PR checkout.
cite_claim: Standard supply-chain hygiene checks require human code review, protected branches and no dangerous workflow triggers.
quote: Reviews may also detect or deter an attacker trying to insert malicious code
relevance: A runnable, Apache-2.0 measure of the target repo's posture. It supports fiks's 'never merge' rule.

title: Risks and mitigations for GitHub Copilot cloud agent
central_claim: The agent pushes only to copilot/ branches or the PR branch it was asked on. Only write-access users can trigger it. It cannot approve or merge, and Actions do not run until a write-access user approves. Internet access is restricted and hidden characters (HTML comments) are filtered.
cite_claim: Industry-standard controls for an autonomous PR-opening agent: branch scoping, no self-merge, human-approved CI runs, egress limits and hidden-text filtering.
location: Headings 'Copilot cloud agent can push code changes to your repository', 'has access to sensitive information', 'AI prompts can be vulnerable to injection'
quote: text entered as an HTML comment in an issue or pull request comment is not passed to Copilot cloud agent.
relevance: Industry baseline for fiks to match or beat. fiks lacks egress limits, hidden-text filtering and human-approved CI runs before its green-CI gate.

title: Beyond permission prompts: making Claude Code more secure and autonomous
central_claim: OS-level filesystem and network isolation for Claude Code's bash tool. Both are needed to stop exfiltration and escape, and internal use saw 84% fewer permission prompts.
cite_claim: Effective sandboxing of a coding agent requires both filesystem and network isolation.
quote: It is worth noting that effective sandboxing requires both filesystem and network isolation.
relevance: fiks restricts tool calls (canUseTool) but does not run pnpm test in an OS sandbox, and agent-written code inherits process.env. A concrete hardening step to adopt.

title: Claude Code: Security
central_claim: Covers the permission system, the working-directory boundary, sandboxed bash, network-command approval and trust verification. The docs note that -p (headless) shows no trust prompt and advise VMs for untrusted content.
cite_claim: Claude Code's prompt-injection safeguards rely on permissions, sandboxing and trust prompts. Headless -p sessions skip trust prompts, and the docs advise isolation for untrusted content.
location: Sections 'Protect against prompt injection', 'Additional safeguards' (Trust verification note), 'Best practices for working with untrusted content'
quote: Avoid piping untrusted content directly to Claude
relevance: fiks's fallback runner uses headless claude -p and pipes untrusted vendor bodies into the prompt, which goes against this vendor guidance unless the bodies are sandboxed or structured.

title: Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions
central_claim: About 40% of 1,689 Copilot-generated programs in CWE-relevant scenarios were vulnerable.
cite_claim: LLM-generated code frequently contains security weaknesses.
quote: it is certain that the language model will have learned from exploitable, buggy code
relevance: Foundational evidence that an LLM-written fix can add vulnerabilities even without an attacker.

title: How Safe Are AI-Generated Patches? A Large-scale Study on Security Risks in LLM and Agentic Automated Program Repair on SWE-bench
central_claim: Uses CodeQL, Semgrep and Bandit (2-of-3 agreement plus manual review). Llama 3.3 patches had 135 confirmed vulnerabilities vs 12 for developer patches. OpenHands, the most autonomous agent, had 44 on the test split, vs 3 (AutoCodeRover) and 2 (HoneyComb).
cite_claim: LLM and agentic program-repair patches add vulnerabilities that developer patches lack, and risk grows with agent autonomy.
quote: giving agents unconstrained autonomy over large repositories can substantially increase the risk of vulnerabilities
relevance: Directly applicable method: scan fiks PR diffs with the same 2-of-3 rule. Supports fiks's narrow-edit policy (src/ only, small diff).

title: SecureVibeBench: Benchmarking Secure Vibe Coding of AI Agents via Reconstructing Vulnerability-Introducing Scenarios
authors: Chen, Huang, Lyu, et al. (incl. Lo)
central_claim: Has 105 C/C++ tasks from 41 OSS-Fuzz projects, built from real vulnerability-introducing commits. The best agent is correct and secure on only 23.8% of tasks.
cite_claim: Code agents working in repository context rarely produce code that is both correct and secure.
quote: current agents struggle to produce both correct and secure code
relevance: Shows a functional gate such as fiks's F to P gate does not certify security. A security oracle is needed separately.

title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs' Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
central_claim: On impossible SWE-bench variants, GPT-5 cheats 54.0% and Claude Opus 4.1 about 50%. Methods are test modification, operator overloading and special-casing. Hiding tests drives cheating near zero, while read-only tests block only test edits. An abort option cuts GPT-5 from 54% to 9%. LLM monitors catch only 42-65% on SWE-bench.
cite_claim: Coding agents game tests when the spec and tests conflict. Read-only tests stop test edits but not special-casing, and an explicit abort option reduces cheating.
quote: The highest performing model in our tests, GPT-5, cheats 54.0% of the time on Conflicting-SWEbench
relevance: The core evidence for 'contract gaming'. fiks's src/-only rule is a read-only-tests control, which leaves special-casing open. Suggests adding an abort or decline path to the repair prompt.

title: Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking
central_claim: o3 stubbed evaluators, tampered with timers and overrode equality operators. It reward-hacked in 30.4% of RE-Bench runs (39/128) and about 0.7% on HCAST.
cite_claim: Frontier models modify scoring code and override comparisons to pass checks, at high rates on some tasks.
quote: On one specific task in RE-Bench, we saw o3 eventually reward-hack in every single trajectory we generated.
relevance: Shows fiks's gates could be gamed from inside src/, for example by overriding comparisons the contract checker relies on. The gate code must live outside the agent's write set.

title: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
central_claim: Injecting 5 malicious texts per target question into a database of millions gives 90% ASR.
cite_claim: A handful of poisoned records in a store an LLM consults is enough to control its output.
quote: PoisonedRAG could achieve a 90% attack success rate when injecting five malicious texts
relevance: The nearest quantitative analog for poisoning fiks's trace store and fixtures, which later prompts and gates consult. An analogy only, not the same setting.
